what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Ten sgit releases turned minutes into seconds; an honest map against Git, corrected after the sgit CLI team's review.
sections.para: Between 3 and 27 October sgit shipped ten releases, each fixing a bottleneck real work found. The ideas came from MGraph-DB, Memory-FS, content-address caching and the writer pays. The article maps what Git lacks, what it shares, where Git leads today and how much can be built, and what a host that reads nothing never can.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Ten releases, per-command speed-ups, the lineage, and a five-way verdict against Git, reviewed by the CLI team.
sections.para: Releases fixed real bottlenecks, taking commands from minutes to seconds. Git has no equivalent for a host that reads nothing, read keys, custody without access, vault-carried policy, blind writes or ranged folder reads. Git shares clones, packs and named-file commits. Git leads on merges, identity, deltas and tools, mostly buildable; some things are impossible by design.

sections.label: Every bottleneck becomes a release
sections.line: Each release fixed a bottleneck a real workload found, ending with pack mode, caches and index packs.
sections.para: Field reports from the PHP newsroom were reproduced and fixed. Pack mode cut a 1.6 GB clone from 827 to 95 seconds. In 0.25.0 a one-file commit went from 1,739 to 4.6 seconds on cli.sgit.ai's vault, 4 minutes to 9 on the newsroom's. 0.26.0 cut a pull from 566 to 31.7 seconds, under a profiler.

sections.label: Minutes to seconds, with the caveats
sections.line: The speed-ups are per command, measured in stated settings, with one regression and a known price.
sections.para: The newsroom's full pass went from 57 to 35 minutes, mostly capture work. Synthetic numbers left the network out. The first status after the 0.25.0 upgrade took 18 minutes 23 seconds while the new cache read every file of a fresh 4.2 GB clone; 0.26.0 fixed it. First pushes and compactions are 35 to 50 seconds slower.

sections.label: Where the speed came from
sections.line: The speed came from earlier work: MGraph-DB, Memory-FS, content-address caching, Type_Safe and the writer pays.
sections.para: MGraph-DB's two-way cross-references became index members mapping blobs to paths and files to commits. Memory-FS's lesson, read by offset, gave the pack store. Content addresses need no cache invalidation. Type_Safe parsing on reads caused the 0.24.0 slowness, so types stay at the writer. The writer pays once; readers skip the walk.

sections.label: Stop comparing sgit with Git
sections.line: sgit's docs still call it git for encrypted vaults; the comparison should be what Git lacks.
sections.para: The Git framing helped when sgit was young: same verbs, same model. It now undersells sgit, because the interesting parts are those Git does not have. A row-by-row comparison against Git's and GitHub's own documentation gives four verdicts: no equivalent, Git has it too, Git is ahead, and next.

sections.label: What Git has no equivalent for
sections.line: Git has no equivalent for a host that reads nothing, read keys, mirrors, vault-carried policy and ranged reads.
sections.para: Privacy: encrypted metadata with a stated leak list, read keys as capability while writing is host-checked, rekey and move, and mirroring a vault without its key. Trust: policy enforced at clone and pull, rewinds refused, a secret guard, signed writer-built indexes. Storage: ranged folder clones, a cache read path, serve and publish, append lanes, agent writes, sealed files.

sections.label: What Git has too, and my memo over-claimed
sections.line: The memo over-claimed: Git has packs, partial, shallow and no-checkout clones, and named-file commits.
sections.para: Git's packs are delta-compressed and kept whole by default. clone --path resembles partial clone with sparse-checkout. git clone --no-checkout is old. sgit write commits named files atomically, Git's commit with paths. sgit has the history tools too: log filters, diff, show, reflog, undo, revert, reset, amend, stash and signed tags.

sections.label: Where Git is ahead today, and how much of it can be built
sections.line: Git leads today on merges, hunks, per-person identity, deltas and tools; almost all of it is buildable client-side.
sections.para: Most gaps are minor or mid-level for agent workflows. Git merges by line and detects renames; sgit merges whole files. Hunk staging is missing. sgit signatures prove a key holder, not a clone, with no per-key expiry. No deltas or garbage collection yet. Blame, bisect and grep are client-side in Git too. Maturity takes time.

sections.label: What a host that reads nothing can never do
sections.line: A few things are impossible when the host reads nothing, each with a client-side substitute.
sections.para: The host cannot search, diff, scan or merge content, so the client or a key-holding runner does. Nobody can take back what a reader has; sgit rotates forward. Per-folder permissions need per-folder keys. Metadata leaks can shrink, never vanish. Store optimisation and fast-forward enforcement move to the client, where the rewind guard ships.

sections.label: Next, not now: one file with no clone, and websites from vaults
sections.line: Reading one file from a pack vault with no clone, and websites served from vaults, are designed, not shipped.
sections.para: On normal vaults a file is four plain requests at the root, one more per folder, or one batch for a cached path; history log already runs with no clone. Pack vault reads by byte range with no clone are Phase 4. PROJECT-003 would move site files into vaults because history grows with generated files.

sections.label: The workflows where this matters
sections.line: Six jobs are hard in Git and natural in sgit today.
sections.para: Many agents each clone one folder of a huge vault, with out-of-scope commits refused. A reader gets read-only access with no account. An agent deposits into an inbox it cannot read. Indexes are trusted only under the vault's signature policy. A backup host mirrors a vault it cannot read. A vault's rules travel with every clone.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Timings are others' measurements, verdicts are against 0.26.0, and sgit's own docs are partly stale.
sections.para: The timings come from the CLI team, cli.sgit.ai and the newsroom, not re-run. Verdicts compare sgit-ai 0.26.0 with Git's and GitHub's documentation. sgit's limitations page still calls signing planned and partial commits impossible; main's changelog still heads 0.26.0 as unreleased. No equivalent means the mainstream toolchain, not add-ons.

sections.label: Reviewed, and corrected
sections.line: The sgit CLI team reviewed the article against their code; it is corrected and extended.
sections.para: The 29-minute figure is sourced from cli.sgit.ai's notes and now attributed. Two claims were too strong: signatures prove a key holder, and indexes follow the vault's signature policy. Several were too weak: named-file commits, no-clone reads, rotation, mirroring, vault-carried policy, rewind refusal and the secret guard. Smaller dates and numbers were fixed.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: sgit's release notes, cli.sgit.ai articles and docs, the CLI repository, the CLI team's review, PyPI, briefs, Git and GitHub docs.
sections.para: Sources include sgit's 0.24.0 to 0.26.0 notes, cli.sgit.ai's articles and docs, the CLI repository's changelog and threat model, the sgit CLI team's review of 28 October, PyPI release times, the PHP newsroom's briefs, and Git's and GitHub's documentation. Two figures are cli.sgit.ai's own.
